title: Empiric antibiotic selection for sepsis
definition: Selecting appropriate empiric antimicrobial coverage considering resistance patterns, allergy history, prior cultures, renal function, and local antibiogram data.
example_ed: 70yo with chronic UTIs presenting with recurrent symptoms. Prior resistance to fluoroquinolones. Which empiric regimen?
example_primary_care: 65yo with cellulitis not responding to first-line oral antibiotics. Escalate outpatient vs. IV antibiotics vs. ED referral?
source_of_variability: Local resistance patterns; guideline variation; allergy history complexity
encounter_frequency: High Sepsis is among the most common serious ED and inpatient presentations; empiric antibiotic decisions required on nearly every sepsis case
error_rate_given_exposure: Medium Suboptimal empiric selection documented; 5% absolute mortality difference between regimens (Chanderraj 2024); variation driven by resistance pattern knowledge gaps
notes: QIAN ET AL JAMA ACORN STUDY--NO DIFFERENCE ZOSYN VS. CEFEPIME
review_scenario: A 70-year-old with recurrent urinary infections presents with fever, dysuria, and hypotension. Prior cultures showed fluoroquinolone resistance, and you need to choose empiric antibiotics before new culture data return.

title: ED disposition decisions (admit vs. discharge) & PCP triage to ED decision-making
definition: Determining appropriate level of care for patients with borderline presentations where both admission and discharge are defensible. Primary care determination of whether a patient requires emergency evaluation vs. can be safely managed outpatient with available resources.
example_ed: CHF exacerbation, sat 91% on room air, chronically ill, poor outpatient follow-up. Admit vs. discharge with close follow-up?
example_primary_care: 28yo with migraine history and new sensory changes to hand. Send to ED for stroke eval? Office neuro exam normal.
source_of_variability: Social determinants + follow-up reliability + risk tolerance variation Limited testing/imaging available; variable risk tolerance; medicolegal pressure
encounter_frequency: High Disposition decisions required for every ED patient; borderline cases estimated at 20-30% of ED volume. PCP-to-ED referral decisions occur daily in primary care; among the most consequential routine decisions in outpatient practice
error_rate_given_exposure: Medium Clinician variation in disposition persists even with validated risk scores; no single benchmark error rate but significant inter-provider disagreement documented (Liu 2021) 11-56% inappropriate ED referral rate documented across studies (Posocco 2017); wide range reflects variability in risk tolerance and available resources
review_scenario: A patient with heart failure presents with dyspnea, borderline oxygen saturation, and limited outpatient support. The workup is reassuring enough that discharge is possible, but the risk of decompensation after going home is not trivial.

title: Chronic disease medication titration
definition: Adjusting medications for chronic conditions when patients present with suboptimal control, requiring integration of acute context, chronic trajectory, and outpatient follow-up reliability.
example_ed: Patient in ED with BP 170s, chronically on BP meds, negative workup. Increase amlodipine before discharge?
example_primary_care: Diabetic with A1c 8.5 on metformin + glipizide. Add third agent vs. insulin? Patient preference vs. guideline.
source_of_variability: Therapeutic inertia bias; acute vs. chronic framing; ownership ambiguity
encounter_frequency: High Chronic disease management is the dominant activity of primary care; medication titration decisions arise at the majority of follow-up visits
error_rate_given_exposure: High Therapeutic inertia documented in up to 40% of hypertensive CKD patients not at goal despite repeated visits (Desai 2013); pervasive across diabetes, heart failure, lipid management
notes: Inpatient data--but Anderson et al argue don't start new antihypertensives for most patients https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/37252732/
review_scenario: A patient with longstanding hypertension is seen after several visits with persistently poor control despite taking multiple medications. You need to decide whether to intensify treatment now or defer changes until there is better follow-up and more context.

title: Medication reconciliation in polypharmacy
definition: Identifying harmful drug interactions, redundancies, and deprescribing opportunities in patients on multiple medications. >90% CDS alert override rate due to fatigue.
example_ed: 60yo admitted with confusion on diuretics, benzodiazepines, and sleeping pills. Which medications are contributing? What to hold?
example_primary_care: 80yo on 14 medications presenting for wellness visit. Statin + new muscle pain. Deprescribing cascade risk.
source_of_variability: Alert fatigue; ownership ambiguity (who is the prescriber?); deprescribing reluctance
encounter_frequency: High Polypharmacy affects >40% of older adults; medication reconciliation required at every care transition
error_rate_given_exposure: High Reconciliation errors at transitions of care are among the most common medication safety events; adverse drug events reduced significantly by structured reconciliation (Jost 2021)
review_scenario: A 60-year-old is admitted with confusion after taking several chronic medications, including a benzodiazepine, a diuretic, and a sedating sleep aid. You need to determine which drugs may be contributing and what should be held, continued, or deprescribed.

title: Test result follow-up and closed-loop tracking
definition: Ensuring abnormal results are communicated, acted upon, and tracked to completion. 6.8% abnormal labs and 7.1% abnormal imaging lack follow-up (Singh); present in 20-30% of ambulatory malpractice claims.
example_ed: Aortic dilation to 5.2cm on CT — when can patient follow up? Who tracks this?
example_primary_care: Mildly elevated liver enzymes on routine labs. Repeat vs. workup? Ensure patient returns.
source_of_variability: System fragmentation; handoff failures; variable EHR tracking tools
encounter_frequency: High Abnormal results generated daily across every clinical setting; closed-loop tracking required for every ordered test
error_rate_given_exposure: High 6.8% of abnormal labs and 7.1% of abnormal imaging lack documented follow-up (Singh); present in 20-30% of ambulatory malpractice claims
review_scenario: A CT ordered for one complaint reveals a serious incidental abnormality that will need follow-up after discharge. You need to decide how urgently it must be addressed, who is responsible for the follow-up plan, and how to make sure it does not get lost.

title: Low-value care avoidance (imaging/testing)
definition: Deciding against testing/imaging when clinical evidence doesn't support it, despite medicolegal pressure or patient expectations. 6.8% abnormal labs and 7.1% abnormal imaging lack follow-up.
example_ed: Does this pediatric bronchiolitis patient really need a chest X-ray?
example_primary_care: Back pain <6 weeks, no red flags. Patient insists on MRI. Order it or not?
source_of_variability: Defensive medicine; patient expectation pressure; medicolegal anxiety
encounter_frequency: High Imaging and testing decisions arise in nearly every clinical encounter; low-value ordering is a system-wide challenge
error_rate_given_exposure: High Imaging overuse estimated at 20-50% of orders in some categories; significant variation across providers even for same presentations (Litkowski 2016)
review_scenario: A child with bronchiolitis is stable and clinically consistent with a viral illness, but the family is asking for a chest X-ray for reassurance. You need to decide whether additional testing would help or would only add cost, radiation, and follow-up burden.

title: Opioid prescribing for discharged patients
definition: Balancing adequate pain control against addiction risk, diversion, and regulatory scrutiny when prescribing opioids at discharge or in the outpatient setting.
example_ed: Kidney stone patient with pain controlled in ED. Prescribe opioids for home? How many? Any history check?
example_primary_care: Chronic low back pain patient requesting opioid refill. PDMP check shows multiple prescribers.
source_of_variability: Risk tolerance + follow-up reliability; pain assessment subjectivity; patient expectation pressure
encounter_frequency: Medium Opioid prescribing at ED discharge occurs in a meaningful subset of ED visits; less frequent in primary care with chronic pain excluded
error_rate_given_exposure: High High inter-provider variability in opioid prescribing documented; prescribing patterns driven by habit and patient pressure more than clinical criteria (Drendel 2020, Mok 2020)
review_scenario: A patient with acute renal colic improves in the emergency department and is ready for discharge. You need to decide whether to prescribe opioids for home use, how much to give, and what risk factors should change that plan.

title: Resource allocation and triage under constraints
definition: Determining intensity of workup, monitoring, and intervention based on competing demands, limited resources, and illness severity.
example_ed: Multiple patients boarding. Which need frequent reassessment vs. can wait? Only one CT slot available.
example_primary_care: End of day, 3 patients need callbacks for abnormal labs. Prioritizing by severity with limited time.
source_of_variability: Highly context-dependent; institutional resource variation; cognitive load from multitasking
encounter_frequency: Medium Formal resource constraint triage occurs during surge conditions, mass casualty events, and high-census periods; not a daily occurrence in stable systems
error_rate_given_exposure: Medium Errors under constraint conditions are underreported; cognitive overload in surge settings well documented but error rates difficult to quantify prospectively (Hick 2011)
notes: Broad — panel may want to narrow or merge with M2
review_scenario: The department is full, several patients are boarding, and only one CT slot is immediately available. You need to decide which patients require the closest reassessment and which limited resources should go to whom first.

title: Goals-concordant care in acute deterioration
clinical_cluster: 5 - Goals of Care and Patient Preference Alignment
definition: Aligning acute treatment decisions with patient preferences and goals of care when the patient cannot participate in real-time decision-making.
example_ed: DNR/DNI patient with reversible hypoxia. BiPAP consistent with goals? Family disagrees.
example_primary_care: Advanced cancer patient with new pneumonia. Aggressive treatment vs. comfort per prior discussions? Documentation unclear.
source_of_variability: Advance directive interpretation; family vs. documented wishes; prognostic uncertainty
encounter_frequency: Medium Acute deterioration requiring goals of care alignment occurs regularly in inpatient and ED settings; less frequent in stable primary care
error_rate_given_exposure: High ICU treatments near end of life frequently not goal-concordant; goals of care documented but not acted upon in significant proportion of cases (Cardona 2020)
notes: Bridges management + communication — panel decides where it fits best
review_scenario: A patient with advanced illness develops acute respiratory distress, and the chart documents DNR/DNI status but little detail about acceptable escalation. The family wants everything done, while the bedside team is unsure which treatments are still consistent with the patient’s goals.

title: Managing contradictory guidelines in multimorbid patients
definition: Navigating treatment decisions when evidence-based guidelines for one condition conflict with guidelines for a co-existing condition, requiring integration of competing risks and benefits.
example_ed: Septic patient with CHF — fluid resuscitation guideline conflicts with volume restriction. Beta-blocker for AFib RVR in patient with acute asthma.
example_primary_care: CHF patient with CKD and diabetes — SGLT2 inhibitor recommended by cardiology, nephrology concerned about AKI, endocrine wants to add it. Whose guideline wins?
source_of_variability: Guideline proliferation without multimorbidity guidance; specialist siloing; no standard for adjudicating conflicts
encounter_frequency: High Multimorbidity affects >60% of adults over 65; guideline conflicts arise in the majority of complex chronic disease management encounters
error_rate_given_exposure: High Most clinical guidelines developed for single-disease populations; conflict rate in multimorbid patients not precisely quantified but considered near-universal in geriatric and complex care (Wunderle 2023)
notes: Affects majority of elderly patients — guidelines written for single-disease populations
review_scenario: A septic patient with heart failure and chronic kidney disease needs urgent treatment, but the guideline-concordant plan for one condition increases risk for the others. You need to choose a management strategy when multiple specialty recommendations point in different directions.

title: Predicting clinical deterioration and acting preemptively
definition: Recognizing early signals of impending deterioration and initiating management before the patient meets formal criteria for intervention. Requires pattern recognition from experience rather than protocol adherence.
example_ed: Patient with borderline vitals and 'looking sick' — not yet meeting sepsis criteria but experienced clinician starts antibiotics early. Intubation setup for the patient who isn't yet in respiratory failure but is trending that way.
example_primary_care: Patient with stable CHF whose weight is trending up 2lbs/week for 3 weeks — intervene now or wait for symptoms? Diabetic with gradually worsening renal function — when to refer nephrology?
source_of_variability: Expert-novice gap is largest here; AI could surface trends physicians miss in data-dense environments
encounter_frequency: High Clinical deterioration recognition is a continuous background task in inpatient and ED care; required across all acuity levels
error_rate_given_exposure: High Early warning score sensitivity 73.9% with human recognition as the limiting factor; failure to rescue from preventable deterioration is a leading inpatient safety event (Miranda 2017)
notes: Separates expert from novice reasoning — fascinating AI teaming question
review_scenario: A patient looks unwell and has borderline vital signs but does not yet meet formal criteria for ICU transfer or a sepsis bundle. You need to decide whether to intervene early based on pattern recognition or wait for clearer objective deterioration.

title: Undifferentiated chest pain risk stratification
clinical_cluster: 2 - High-Risk Diagnostic Rule Out / Uncertainty Management
definition: Determining disposition and workup for patients whose risk factors place them in an intermediate-risk category, requiring synthesis of history, ECG, labs, and risk scores. 47% physician difficulty rate; top malpractice claim; 2-4x physician variation.
example_ed: 45yo M with atypical chest pain, normal ECG, mildly elevated troponin. ACS vs. dissection vs. musculoskeletal. Admit vs. obs vs. discharge?
example_primary_care: 55yo F with exertional chest tightness and 2 cardiac risk factors. Office ECG normal. Send to ED vs. stress test outpatient vs. reassurance?
source_of_variability: Premature closure dominant error
encounter_frequency: High Chest pain is among the top 3 ED chief complaints nationally; risk stratification required for every presentation
error_rate_given_exposure: Medium HEART score kappa 0.48 between physicians; >25% risk classification disagreement between ED physicians and cardiologists (Wu 2016, Soares 2021)
review_scenario: A 45-year-old with chest pain has a nondiagnostic ECG and only a mild troponin elevation. You need to decide whether this presentation warrants discharge, observation, or a more aggressive workup for a potentially dangerous cause.

title: Sepsis recognition in ambiguous presentations
clinical_cluster: 2 - High-Risk Diagnostic Rule Out / Uncertainty Management
definition: Early identification of SIRS/sepsis in patients with vague symptoms or atypical biomarkers. 7.6% mortality increase per hour of antibiotic delay; SEP-3 sensitivity only 54-70%; bundle compliance 20-70%.
example_ed: Immunocompromised patient with WBC elevation but minimal symptoms and borderline vitals.
example_primary_care: Elderly diabetic with fatigue and mild confusion, afebrile. UTI vs. early sepsis vs. dehydration? Send to ED?
source_of_variability: Time-sensitivity + nonspecific presentations
encounter_frequency: High Sepsis presentations encountered daily in ED and inpatient settings; ambiguous early presentations are the norm not the exception
error_rate_given_exposure: High SEP-3 sensitivity only 54-70%; 7.6% mortality increase per hour of antibiotic delay; missed sepsis a leading cause of preventable inpatient death
notes: Good example, esp. re Epic ML prediction tool. SEP not a great model....
review_scenario: An older immunocompromised patient presents with fatigue, mild confusion, and borderline vital signs but no clear source of infection. You need to decide whether this is early sepsis, a less dangerous process, or something else entirely.

title: Stroke diagnosis including posterior circulation
clinical_cluster: 2 - High-Risk Diagnostic Rule Out / Uncertainty Management
definition: Recognizing stroke presentations including subtle posterior circulation strokes. 9-26% misdiagnosis rate; posterior strokes missed 20-40%; every 15-min delay increases mortality.
example_ed: Elderly female with nystagmus, NIH 0, dizziness. CT imaging equivocal. Stroke protocol + TNK?
example_primary_care: 65yo M with 2 days of episodic vertigo and gait unsteadiness. TIA vs. BPPV? Urgency of imaging?
source_of_variability: Posterior strokes lack classic presentation; anchoring on benign diagnoses
encounter_frequency: Medium Stroke presentations are common in ED but posterior circulation strokes represent ~20% of strokes; atypical presentations seen regularly
error_rate_given_exposure: High Posterior circulation stroke frequently missed by both EM and neurology in ED; miss rates estimated at 35-40% in atypical presentations (Arch 2016)
review_scenario: An older patient presents with dizziness, gait instability, and nystagmus, but the initial imaging is equivocal and the NIH stroke scale is low. You need to decide whether this is a posterior circulation stroke that demands urgent treatment or a less dangerous vestibular process.

title: Pulmonary embolism evaluation
clinical_cluster: 2 - High-Risk Diagnostic Rule Out / Uncertainty Management
definition: Risk-stratifying and evaluating for PE with variable pre-test probability, D-dimer thresholds, and imaging decisions. Missed in ~33% of fatal autopsy cases. top 5 malpractice claim.
example_ed: 32yo F post-partum with pleuritic chest pain and tachycardia. D-dimer elevated. CT-PA vs. V/Q?
example_primary_care: 32yo F on OCPs with shortness of breath in clinic. Should she be sent to the ER?
source_of_variability: Subjective pretest probability + variable D-dimer thresholds; imaging threshold shaped by fear of missed diagnosis / medicolegal risk
encounter_frequency: High PE evaluation required across a wide range of presentations in ED and primary care; among the most common diagnostic dilemmas
error_rate_given_exposure: Medium Structured algorithms reduce CT-PA ordering ~11% without increasing missed PE (Ehrman 2021); over- and under-testing both documented; clinical gestalt unreliable alone
review_scenario: A postpartum patient presents with pleuritic chest pain, tachycardia, and shortness of breath. You need to judge the likelihood of pulmonary embolism and choose the next diagnostic step without exposing the patient to unnecessary testing.

title: Pediatric abdominal pain evaluation
clinical_cluster: 2 - High-Risk Diagnostic Rule Out / Uncertainty Management
definition: Determining appropriate workup intensity for children with abdominal pain, balancing diagnostic yield against radiation/procedural risk.
example_ed: 4yo with abnormal vitals, holding stomach. CT vs. ultrasound vs. observation? Appendicitis vs. constipation vs. intussusception.
example_primary_care: 8yo with recurrent abdominal pain and weight loss. Functional vs. IBD vs. celiac? When to image?
source_of_variability: Radiation risk aversion vs. miss risk; variable imaging thresholds by institution
encounter_frequency: Medium Pediatric abdominal pain is a frequent ED presentation; appendicitis evaluation required in a meaningful subset
error_rate_given_exposure: Medium Ultrasound sensitivity only 38% for appendicitis; CT superior but radiation risk creates decision complexity; CDR reduces CT use ~20% (Gregory 2016, Abo 2011)
notes: Confirm pediatric tasks in scope
review_scenario: A young child presents with abdominal pain, abnormal vital signs, and limited ability to explain the symptoms. You need to decide how aggressively to evaluate for a surgical emergency while minimizing unnecessary radiation or invasive testing.

title: Altered mental status workup
clinical_cluster: 2 - High-Risk Diagnostic Rule Out / Uncertainty Management
definition: Systematic evaluation of AMS across metabolic, infectious, neurologic, toxic, and psychiatric etiologies when the presentation is undifferentiated.
example_ed: 30yo with substance use history, severely confused, abnormal vitals. Toxic-metabolic vs. CNS infection vs. structural? CT? LP?
example_primary_care: 75yo brought by family for progressive confusion over 2 weeks. UTI vs. medication side effect vs. early dementia vs. subdural?
source_of_variability: Wide differential creates anchoring risk; framing by EMS report biases workup
encounter_frequency: High AMS is among the top 5 ED chief complaints; encountered daily across ED and inpatient medicine
error_rate_given_exposure: High Delirium missed in >50% of older ED patients (Sanders 2002); 84.6% of delirium cases unrecognized in multicenter ED study (Boucher 2019)
review_scenario: A patient with severe confusion, abnormal vital signs, and a history that could fit toxic, infectious, or neurologic causes arrives without a reliable historian. You need to structure the workup quickly while the differential remains broad and high risk.

title: Diagnosis with incomplete or limited data
definition: Evaluating potential diagnoses when standard diagnostic information is unavailable, inadequate, or contraindicated.
example_ed: CT without contrast due to allergies — can you rule out PE? Incomplete hand X-ray series — fracture vs. no fracture?
example_primary_care: Patient declines bloodwork for religious reasons. Assessing anemia clinically only.
source_of_variability: Clinician comfort with uncertainty varies widely; risk tolerance differences
encounter_frequency: High Incomplete data is the default state of clinical practice; rare to have complete information at point of decision
error_rate_given_exposure: Medium Error rates under incomplete data conditions difficult to quantify directly; comfort with uncertainty as a learnable skill suggests significant variability across providers (Ilgen 2019)
notes: might be difficult to get 1000 patient cases for this
review_scenario: A patient may have a serious diagnosis, but the usual confirming data are missing because the key test is incomplete, contraindicated, or declined. You need to decide how much diagnostic confidence is possible with limited information.

title: Imaging and test interpretation with incomplete context
definition: Interpreting diagnostic studies (imaging, ECG, labs) when clinical context is limited or absent. Chest X-ray discordance 20-30%; mammography sensitivity 62-91% across radiologists.
example_ed: ECG arrives in triage with no clinical context. NSTEMI? STEMI? Baseline changes?
example_primary_care: Abnormal mammogram result arrives — patient has implants and prior radiation. True positive vs. artifact?
source_of_variability: Interpreter expertise variation; availability of comparison studies; anchoring on prior reads
encounter_frequency: High Imaging and test interpretation without full clinical context occurs daily; results read without access to complete history is common in radiology and ED workflows
error_rate_given_exposure: Medium Chest X-ray discordance 20-30%; mammography sensitivity 62-91% across radiologists; AI discordance with specialists documented when clinical context absent (Young 2024)
notes: Related to D8 but distinct — D8 is about missing data, D9 is about interpreting data without context
review_scenario: An abnormal test result reaches you with little or no clinical context about why it was ordered or what the patient looked like at the time. You need to decide how much weight to give the finding and what follow-up it should trigger.

title: Undifferentiated symptoms in vulnerable populations
clinical_cluster: 2 - High-Risk Diagnostic Rule Out / Uncertainty Management
definition: Diagnostic reasoning for patients who cannot clearly communicate symptoms or whose presentations are inherently atypical (young children, elderly, cognitively impaired, non-verbal).
example_ed: Pre-verbal toddler with fever, vomiting, abdominal pain. Virus vs. appendicitis vs. intussusception?
example_primary_care: Non-verbal dementia patient with agitation. Pain? UTI? Medication effect? Constipation?
source_of_variability: Communication barriers increase reliance on pattern recognition over history
encounter_frequency: Medium Vulnerable populations (elderly, cognitively impaired, pediatric) represent a significant but not dominant proportion of daily encounters
error_rate_given_exposure: High Atypical presentations in immunocompromised and elderly patients are a leading source of diagnostic delay; missed diagnoses disproportionately concentrated in these populations
notes: Overlaps D6 (peds) and D7 (AMS) — panel should decide scope
review_scenario: A patient from a vulnerable population cannot clearly describe symptoms, and the presentation could reflect either benign illness or a high-risk diagnosis. You need to infer what matters most from sparse or indirect information.

title: High-risk diagnosis confirmation before irreversible intervention
clinical_cluster: 2 - High-Risk Diagnostic Rule Out / Uncertainty Management
definition: Confirming a time-sensitive diagnosis with sufficient confidence to initiate an irreversible or high-risk treatment under time pressure.
example_ed: Acute stroke — sufficient evidence to administer TPA within window? New-onset AFib with RVR — rate control vs. cardioversion?
example_primary_care: Suspected meningitis in child with fever and neck stiffness — start empiric antibiotics before LP results?
source_of_variability: Time pressure compresses analytical reasoning; irreversibility raises stakes of error
encounter_frequency: Low High-stakes irreversible interventions (thrombolytics, emergent surgery, cath lab activation) are lower-frequency events even in high-acuity settings
error_rate_given_exposure: High When errors occur they are catastrophic and irreversible; wrong-patient or wrong-diagnosis thrombolysis and surgery represent the highest-severity diagnostic errors in medicine
notes: Meta-task that overlaps D2, D3 — consider whether this is a dimension rather than a task
review_scenario: A time-sensitive diagnosis is suspected, and the next treatment step could be beneficial if correct but harmful if wrong. You need to decide whether the evidence is strong enough to proceed before certainty is possible.

title: Cancer screening interpretation and follow-up
definition: Interpreting ambiguous screening results (imaging, labs) and determining appropriate follow-up intensity, balancing overdiagnosis against missed early-stage disease.
example_ed: Incidental lung nodule on trauma CT. Follow-up recommendation? Fleischner criteria application.
example_primary_care: PSA 5.2 in a 62yo. Biopsy vs. repeat vs. MRI? Patient anxiety vs. overdiagnosis risk.
source_of_variability: Guideline complexity; variable risk tolerance for watchful waiting vs. intervention
encounter_frequency: High Cancer screening interpretation required across the vast majority of primary care panels; follow-up decisions generated continuously
error_rate_given_exposure: Medium Mammography sensitivity 62-91% across radiologists; follow-up variability for ambiguous findings (BI-RADS 3-4) is well documented; no single error rate but substantial practice variation
notes: Gap identified — high-risk, high-frequency primary care task
review_scenario: A screening or incidental cancer-related result is abnormal but not definitive. You need to decide whether to escalate immediately, repeat testing, or monitor over time while balancing anxiety, overdiagnosis, and missed disease.

title: Incidental finding management
definition: Determining appropriate workup and follow-up for unexpected findings discovered during evaluation for a different clinical question.
example_ed: CT abdomen for appendicitis reveals adrenal mass. Workup now or outpatient? Who follows up?
example_primary_care: Chest X-ray for cough shows small pleural effusion. Pursue further or monitor?
source_of_variability: Handoff failures for incidental findings; variable follow-up infrastructure
encounter_frequency: High Incidental findings generated in a large proportion of imaging studies; estimated >50% of CT scans contain at least one incidental finding
error_rate_given_exposure: High Follow-up rates for incidental findings highly variable across institutions; significant proportion lost to follow-up; no standardized management protocols in most systems (Berland 2010)
notes: Related to D12 but distinct — incidentals are unplanned
review_scenario: A test ordered for one problem unexpectedly reveals a different abnormality that may or may not matter. You need to decide whether to work it up now, arrange outpatient follow-up, or monitor without overreacting.

title: Premature closure after initial diagnosis identified
clinical_cluster: 9 - Cognitive Bias and Diagnostic Error Resistance
definition: Stopping the diagnostic search after identifying an initial finding, missing co-existing conditions, secondary injuries, or alternative diagnoses that explain the full clinical picture.
example_ed: Trauma patient with obvious femur fracture — missed C-spine injury because attention focused on the dramatic finding. Polysubstance OD — treating for opioids, missing concurrent benzodiazepine ingestion.
example_primary_care: Patient with confirmed UTI and dysuria — missed concurrent diabetes diagnosis from glucose on UA. Treating depression, missing hypothyroidism causing same symptoms.
source_of_variability: Cognitive offloading once 'an answer' is found; satisfaction of search well-documented in radiology and EM
encounter_frequency: High Every diagnostic encounter carries risk of premature closure; the cognitive tendency is universal and not confined to specific presentations
error_rate_given_exposure: High Premature closure identified in 58.5% of diagnostic error cases (Watari 2022); contributes to 40-85% of diagnostic errors across specialties
notes: Classic cognitive error — highly benchmarkable with multi-problem vignettes. might be tough to find 1000 cases of this specific task problem. might be better as a dimension
review_scenario: A dramatic diagnosis has already been identified, and the team’s attention is anchored there. You need to decide whether anything important could still be missing despite having already found one obvious explanation.

title: Re-evaluating a working diagnosis when new data contradicts it
clinical_cluster: 9 - Cognitive Bias and Diagnostic Error Resistance
definition: Updating or abandoning an initial diagnostic impression when subsequent information (labs, imaging, clinical trajectory) is inconsistent with the working diagnosis. Requires metacognitive awareness that the initial frame may be wrong.
example_ed: Patient admitted for CHF exacerbation not improving with diuresis — actually a PE. EMS report says 'psych patient' — actually hypoglycemic.
example_primary_care: Treating recurrent 'GERD' for months — actually eosinophilic esophagitis. Attributing fatigue to depression — actually new-onset anemia from colon cancer.
source_of_variability: Anchoring bias is the most studied cognitive bias in medicine; sunk cost of prior workup reinforces original diagnosis
encounter_frequency: High Working diagnosis reassessment required whenever new data arrives; a continuous background cognitive task in every clinical encounter
error_rate_given_exposure: High Anchoring identified in 60% of diagnostic error cases (Watari 2022); failure to update on contradicting data present in ~30% of diagnostic errors in autopsy studies (Croskerry)
notes: Distinct from D14 — premature closure is stopping too early, anchoring is refusing to change course
review_scenario: A patient is being treated for a working diagnosis, but the clinical course and new data no longer fit. You need to decide when to abandon the original frame and reopen the differential.

title: Integrating discordant diagnostic information
clinical_cluster: 9 - Cognitive Bias and Diagnostic Error Resistance
definition: Synthesizing and weighing conflicting signals across data sources (history vs. labs vs. imaging vs. exam) when they point toward different diagnoses, without defaulting to a single data source.
example_ed: Chest pain patient: history suggests ACS, troponin borderline, ECG shows non-specific changes, CT-A shows no PE but incidental finding. Which signal dominates?
example_primary_care: Patient reports feeling fine, A1c is 11, home glucometer readings are all normal. Which data do you trust? Device malfunction vs. non-compliance vs. lab error?
source_of_variability: Clinicians vary in which data source they weight most heavily; no standard hierarchy for conflicting information
encounter_frequency: High Discordant data across history, exam, labs, and imaging is the norm in complex presentations; integration required in nearly every non-straightforward case
error_rate_given_exposure: High HFpEF diagnosis discordant in 50% of cases between testing positions (Fudim 2024); data integration failure is a core mechanism of diagnostic error across specialties
notes: Common daily challenge — AI could help or hurt depending on which signal it amplifies--DJM agree, good hard example.
review_scenario: History, exam, labs, and imaging are pointing in different directions rather than converging on a single answer. You need to decide which signals deserve the most trust and how to integrate the conflicting information into one plan.

title: EHR signal-to-noise filtering under information overload
definition: Identifying clinically relevant findings and red flags within an EHR record saturated with repetitive notes, auto-populated text, redundant alerts, and irrelevant historical entries, requiring active filtering to extract the signal that drives decision-making.
example_ed: Patient presents with chest pain. Chart contains 400+ notes, majority of which are copied forward. Provider must identify the one note from 6 months ago documenting prior cocaine use and QTc prolongation.
example_primary_care: Complex patient with 12 years of records. Must locate prior colonoscopy result and pathology report buried among hundreds of routine visit notes to determine cancer screening interval.
source_of_variability: EHR design and information architecture; note bloat from copy-forward behavior; alert fatigue; provider experience with chart navigation
encounter_frequency: High Heavy EHR use is near-universal; note bloat and alert fatigue documented across all clinical settings; the average ICU physician encounters 100+ alerts per day (van der Sijs 2006)
error_rate_given_exposure: High Alert fatigue contributes to override rates of 49-96% (Slight 2013); missed findings in voluminous records implicated in diagnostic error; information overload cited as a leading contributor to cognitive failures (Singh 2013)
notes: particularly observable in ChatEHR query logs where providers search for buried information
review_scenario: A clinically complex patient has years of copied-forward notes, redundant alerts, and buried key details in the chart. You need to identify the few pieces of information that actually change today’s decision-making.

title: Informed consent under impaired capacity
definition: Obtaining informed consent when decision-making capacity is questionable, requiring simultaneous capacity assessment and risk communication.
example_ed: Intoxicated patient needing laceration repair. Capacity to consent? Proceed vs. wait vs. surrogate?
example_primary_care: Early dementia patient needing to consent to colonoscopy. Understands benefits but not risks.
source_of_variability: Capacity assessment is subjective; urgency vs. autonomy tradeoff
encounter_frequency: Medium Impaired capacity presentations occur regularly in ED and inpatient settings; less common but not rare in primary care
error_rate_given_exposure: High Capacity assessment frequently omitted or performed informally; inadequate assessment documented as contributing factor in consent-related adverse events (Barstow 2018)
review_scenario: An intoxicated patient needs an urgent but non-life-saving procedure and cannot clearly demonstrate understanding of the risks and options. You need to decide whether the patient has capacity, whether treatment can proceed, and whether a surrogate should be involved.

title: Critical diagnosis disclosure and shared decision-making
definition: Communicating a new serious diagnosis while simultaneously engaging the patient in treatment decision-making under emotional distress.
example_ed: Telling a patient their CT shows a large mass concerning for cancer. Next steps in the ED.
example_primary_care: Delivering a new cancer diagnosis at a follow-up visit. Treatment options, prognosis, referrals.
source_of_variability: Framing effects; physician comfort with uncertainty; cultural factors
encounter_frequency: Medium Critical diagnosis disclosure required for every new serious diagnosis; frequency depends on practice setting and specialty
error_rate_given_exposure: High SDM-aligned communication not consistently associated with reduced prognostic misunderstanding in ICU (Vick 2024); patient comprehension of serious diagnoses frequently overestimated by clinicians
review_scenario: You are meeting a patient whose imaging strongly suggests a new cancer diagnosis. In the same conversation, you need to explain the finding, respond to emotion, and help the patient understand the immediate next decisions.

title: Health literacy-adapted communication
definition: Adjusting clinical communication to patient health literacy level while ensuring adequate understanding of diagnosis, treatment plan, and follow-up.
example_ed: Discharging patient with new AFib, anticoagulation instructions, and return precautions.
example_primary_care: Explaining insulin initiation to a patient with limited English proficiency and 4th grade reading level.
source_of_variability: Patient literacy variation; time constraints; interpreter availability
encounter_frequency: High Health literacy adaptation required in the majority of clinical encounters; ~36% of US adults have basic or below basic health literacy
error_rate_given_exposure: High Gaps in health literacy awareness among community clinicians documented; behavior change limited even after training (Hildenbrand 2020, Mor-Anavy 2021)
review_scenario: A patient with limited health literacy needs discharge instructions for a new high-risk condition and a medication that requires careful adherence. You need to explain the plan in a way the patient can actually understand and use at home.

title: Cognitive task interruption and resumption
definition: Returning to a complex cognitive task after an interruption, with risk of losing context, skipping steps, or making errors due to disrupted working memory.
example_ed: Calculating medication dosing for critical patient, interrupted by code blue, then returning to original task.
example_primary_care: Reviewing complex lab panel, interrupted by urgent phone call, resuming review and missing abnormal value.
source_of_variability: Interruption frequency varies by setting; no standard resumption protocols
encounter_frequency: High Interruptions occur multiple times per hour in ED and inpatient settings; task resumption required continuously throughout every shift
error_rate_given_exposure: High 13.5% of ED discharge prescriptions had errors with interruptions as contributing factor (Anzan 2021); physicians underestimate actual interruption frequency (Eng 2019)
notes: Human factors literature strongly supports this
review_scenario: You are calculating a weight-based medication dose for a critically ill patient when a code blue interrupts you. When you return to the original task a few minutes later, you need to resume safely without losing context or skipping a step.

title: ED physician handoffs (shift change)
definition: Transferring critical clinical information at shift change where errors in transmission directly threaten patient safety.
example_ed: Forget to document in EHR and then handoff with no communication. Pending labs, vital sign trends lost.
example_primary_care: Handoff of deteriorating patient to covering physician at end of day. Critical lab pending.
source_of_variability: Nonstandard structure + interruptions + cognitive load; selective info transfer (mental model differences)
encounter_frequency: High Shift-change handoffs occur at least once per shift for every provider; among the highest-frequency structured communication events in medicine
error_rate_given_exposure: High Information loss at handoff is a leading cause of preventable adverse events; I-PASS reduced perceived information loss by 50% suggesting baseline rates are high (Yanni 2023)
notes: Renamed from original — applies beyond ED
review_scenario: At shift change, you are handing off a patient with pending labs, evolving vital sign abnormalities, and an unclear disposition. The next clinician will be making decisions soon, so the key risks and unfinished work need to be communicated accurately.

title: Human-AI disagreement management
definition: Managing the cognitive conflict when AI-generated recommendations contradict the physician's clinical judgment, requiring metacognitive evaluation of both the AI output and one's own reasoning.
example_ed: AI suggests PE workup for a patient you've assessed as low-risk. Override or order CT-PA?
example_primary_care: AI flags a medication interaction you've been prescribing for years without issue. Change practice or dismiss?
source_of_variability: Automation bias; algorithm aversion; no standard for AI override decisions
encounter_frequency: Medium Human-AI disagreement currently occurs in settings with deployed CDS tools; will increase significantly as AI integration expands
error_rate_given_exposure: High Physicians susceptible to ML recommendations especially when less confident; explanation type significantly affects trust calibration (Chen 2024); automation bias well documented
notes: would be tough to get 1000 patient cases for this. might be more of a dimension we can test the clinician-AI team on
review_scenario: A decision-support tool recommends an aggressive workup that conflicts with your own bedside assessment. You need to decide whether to follow the AI recommendation, override it, or gather more data while managing uncertainty about which judgment to trust.

title: Goals of care conversations
definition: Facilitating time-sensitive discussions about treatment goals, code status, and end-of-life preferences, where framing directly impacts patient/family decisions.
example_ed: Critically ill patient in ED, family at bedside. Full code vs. comfort care discussion. Minutes matter for ICU bed.
example_primary_care: Advanced COPD patient with declining function. Initiating advance directive conversation at annual visit.
source_of_variability: Framing effects on patient/family decisions; physician prognostic uncertainty; cultural variation
encounter_frequency: Medium Goals of care conversations required for seriously ill patients; frequency depends heavily on practice setting — daily in palliative care, weekly in general medicine
error_rate_given_exposure: High Clinicians frequently defer conversations; end-of-life communication barriers documented across settings (Brighton 2016); patient and family understanding of prognosis frequently poor
review_scenario: A seriously ill patient is deteriorating, family members are at the bedside, and decisions about code status or escalation cannot wait until later. You need to lead a goals-of-care conversation under time pressure while emotions are high.

title: Patient portal message triage
definition: Triaging and responding to patient-initiated messages that may contain time-sensitive or high-risk clinical information, within a workflow not designed for acute decision-making.
example_ed: ED follow-up message: 'My pain is worse since discharge yesterday and now I have a fever.'
example_primary_care: Patient messages at 9pm: 'I've had chest pain all day but didn't want to bother you.' Seen next morning.
source_of_variability: No standard triage protocols; volume overwhelming; medicolegal uncertainty
encounter_frequency: High Patient portal messages now represent a significant and growing proportion of primary care workload; daily occurrence for most outpatient providers
error_rate_given_exposure: Medium Only 26.8% of oncology portal messages require physician expertise (Anderson 2024); triage errors possible but most messages low acuity; high-risk messages in low-signal environment is the core danger
notes: Added ED parallel — post-discharge messages are increasingly common
review_scenario: An overnight portal message says the patient’s pain is worse after a recent visit and now includes a new fever. You need to decide whether this can wait for routine follow-up or whether it signals a problem that needs urgent escalation.

title: Communicating diagnostic or prognostic uncertainty to patients
definition: Conveying honest uncertainty about diagnosis, prognosis, or treatment effectiveness to patients without eroding trust or causing unnecessary anxiety. Requires calibrating how much uncertainty to share and framing it constructively.
example_ed: Telling a patient: 'Your CT was negative but I can't fully rule out appendicitis. Here are the signs to come back for.' How much uncertainty is too much?
example_primary_care: Explaining to a patient with an indeterminate lung nodule: 'It's probably nothing, but we need to follow it.' Balancing reassurance vs. vigilance.
source_of_variability: Physician comfort with uncertainty varies; patients interpret probabilistic language differently; framing effects on adherence
encounter_frequency: High Uncertainty is present in the majority of clinical encounters; communicating it to patients is a continuous and underrecognized task
error_rate_given_exposure: High Clinicians frequently avoid explicit uncertainty communication; patients frequently misinterpret clinical uncertainty as incompetence; structured frameworks rarely used in practice (Downer 2021)
notes: Directly relevant to AI-generated risk scores that physicians need to translate for patients
review_scenario: The workup is reassuring but not definitive, and you cannot fully exclude a dangerous diagnosis. You need to explain the remaining uncertainty honestly while still giving the patient a clear plan and preserving trust.

title: Establishing shared understanding with consultants and teams
definition: Ensuring that the receiving clinician (consultant, admitting team, specialist) has the same understanding of the clinical situation, urgency, and decision rationale as the referring clinician.
example_ed: Calling cardiology for a NSTEMI consult — your concern is RV strain, their mental model is 'another troponin leak.' Different urgency, different plan.
example_primary_care: Referring to GI for elevated liver enzymes — you're worried about autoimmune hepatitis, GI assumes fatty liver and schedules routine follow-up in 3 months.
source_of_variability: Mental model divergence between teams; loss of clinical reasoning context in referral; specialty-specific framing biases
encounter_frequency: High Consultant communication required multiple times daily in ED and inpatient settings; shared mental model failures are a continuous risk
error_rate_given_exposure: High Shared mental model failures identified as core contributor to team-based care errors; high-performing teams distinguished by explicit model-building behaviors (Gregory 2021)
notes: Where cognitive tasks cross team boundaries — high error rate at these interfaces
review_scenario: You call a consultant because you are worried about a high-risk process, but the receiving team seems to view the case as routine. You need to communicate the urgency and your mental model clearly enough that both teams are acting on the same problem.

title: History elicitation under patient communication barriers
definition: Obtaining a reliable clinical history from patients with impaired communication due to cognitive dysfunction, altered mental status, language barriers, low health literacy, or psychiatric overlay, requiring triangulation across multiple sources to reconstruct accurate clinical narrative.
example_ed: Elderly patient with dementia presents via EMS with altered behavior. No family available. History requires synthesis of EMS report, nursing home records, and limited patient responses.
example_primary_care: Non-English-speaking patient with poorly controlled diabetes presents for follow-up. Interpreter unavailable. Must elicit medication adherence, symptoms, and social history through limited means.
source_of_variability: Language concordance; interpreter availability; cognitive impairment severity; collateral source availability
encounter_frequency: High Impaired history elicitation occurs across a substantial proportion of ED and primary care encounters; estimated 20-30% of ED patients have communication barriers (e.g., altered mental status, language, dementia)
error_rate_given_exposure: High Diagnostic errors attributable to inadequate history have been documented in up to 78% of missed diagnoses (Graber 2005); communication barriers independently associated with adverse events (Divi 2007)
review_scenario: A patient with limited ability to communicate arrives without a reliable historian, and the available story is fragmented across EMS, prior records, and partial patient responses. You need to reconstruct the history well enough to guide care despite those barriers.
